Adding scenarios to our app



A common use for a DES app is to compare scenarios with different inputs.
Our current app shows results for one run at a time. Changing the inputs and running again replaces the previous results.






To compare scenarios, we need to:

Save each run’s inputs and results.
Allow users to view and compare saved scenarios.

section: Two pages: run scenarios and explore results
text:
Two pages: run scenarios and explore results
As shown, our app now splits the original simulation page into two:

Run simulation: set inputs and run the model.
View results: view results from a saved scenario or compare several.



Why?
These pages support two different tasks: setting up simulations and making sense of their results. Users can move between them without having to do both in the same place.
This keeps the interface manageable if we add more inputs, results and comparison features.

New dictionary in session state


We’ll initialise the dictionary in app.py, which runs before whichever page the user opens.

Why not in simulation.py?
Users might open the results page before running a simulation. If we created the dictionary only in simulation.py, it wouldn’t exist yet, causing an error.
Putting this code in app.py ensures the dictionary exists before either page needs it.

"""Entrypoint for app. Defines navigation."""

import streamlit as st

# Initialise session state before running any page
if "scenarios" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.scenarios = {}

pg = st.navigation(
    [
        st.Page("home.py", title="Home"),
        st.Page("simulation.py", title="Run simulation"),
    ]
)

pg.run()

Run and save the results


In simulation.py, we’ll keep the code that sets the inputs and runs the simulation.
We’ll remove the analysis code for now and move it to the results page later. We can also remove import plotly.express as px as this page no longer uses it.

We’ll add new code to:

Name the scenario
Save its settings and results in st.session_state.scenarios.


"""Simple single-page app."""

import streamlit as st
from model import Param, Trial


DEFAULTS = {
    "mean_patient_inter": 5.0,
    "mean_nurse_consult_time": 6.0,
    "sd_nurse_consult_time": 1.0,
    "num_nurses": 1,
    "nurse_cost_per_hour": 30.0,
    "sim_duration": 120,
    "num_replications": 30,
}


def reset_widgets():
    for key, value in DEFAULTS.items():
        st.session_state[key] = value


with st.container(border=True):
    st.subheader("Patients")

    st.slider(
        label="Mean patient inter-arrival time (minutes)",
        min_value=3.0,
        max_value=7.0,
        value=DEFAULTS["mean_patient_inter"],
        step=0.25,
        key="mean_patient_inter",
    )

    st.subheader("Nurses")

    mean_col, sd_col = st.columns(2)

    with mean_col:
        st.number_input(
            label="Mean consultation length (minutes)",
            min_value=3.0,
            max_value=9.0,
            value=DEFAULTS["mean_nurse_consult_time"],
            key="mean_nurse_consult_time",
        )

    with sd_col:
        st.number_input(
            label="Standard deviation of consultation length (minutes)",
            min_value=0.0,
            value=DEFAULTS["sd_nurse_consult_time"],
            key="sd_nurse_consult_time",
        )

    st.pills(
        label="Number of nurses",
        options=range(1, 5),
        default=DEFAULTS["num_nurses"],
        key="num_nurses"
    )

    st.number_input(
        label="Cost per nurse per hour (£)",
        min_value=0.0,
        value=DEFAULTS["nurse_cost_per_hour"],
        step=1.0,
        key="nurse_cost_per_hour",
        help="Nurses are costed for the full simulation duration, including time when they are not seeing patients",
    )

    st.space(size="xxsmall")
    st.subheader("Simulation")

    st.slider(
        label="Simulation duration (minutes)",
        min_value=50,
        max_value=200,
        value=DEFAULTS["sim_duration"],
        key="sim_duration",
    )

    st.slider(
        label="Number of replications",
        min_value=10,
        max_value=50,
        value=DEFAULTS["num_replications"],
        key="num_replications",
    )

with st.container(horizontal=True):
    run = st.button("Run and save scenario", type="primary")
    st.button("Reset to defaults", on_click=reset_widgets)

if run:
    params = Param(
        mean_patient_inter=st.session_state.mean_patient_inter,
        mean_nurse_consult_time=st.session_state.mean_nurse_consult_time,
        sd_nurse_consult_time=st.session_state.sd_nurse_consult_time,
        num_nurses=st.session_state.num_nurses,
        sim_duration=st.session_state.sim_duration,
        num_replications=st.session_state.num_replications,
        nurse_cost_per_hour=st.session_state.nurse_cost_per_hour,
    )
    trial = Trial(param=params)
    trial.run_trial()
    trial.calculate_trial_results()

    # Save results to session state to allow comparison between scenarios
    scenario_name = f"Scenario {len(st.session_state.scenarios) + 1}"
    st.session_state.scenarios[scenario_name] = {
        "settings": {
            "Scenario": scenario_name,
            "Inter-arrival": st.session_state.mean_patient_inter,
            "Consultation mean": st.session_state.mean_nurse_consult_time,
            "Consultation SD": st.session_state.sd_nurse_consult_time,
            "Nurses": st.session_state.num_nurses,
            "Cost per hour": st.session_state.nurse_cost_per_hour,
            "Duration": st.session_state.sim_duration,
            "Replications": st.session_state.num_replications,
        },
        "mean": trial.trial_mean_q_time_nurse,
        "sd": trial.trial_sd_q_time_nurse,
        "p90": trial.trial_perc_90_q_time_nurse,
        "se": trial.se_q_time_nurse,
        "ci_lower": trial.ci_lower_q_time_nurse,
        "ci_upper": trial.ci_upper_q_time_nurse,
        "cost": trial.total_nurse_cost,
        "df": trial.replication_df,
    }

Run and save the results
We then set chosen_scenario to this scenario, making it the default selection when the user opens the results page.
We also show a success message to confirm that the scenario has run and its results have been saved.

Keeping track of scenarios
We can also show a table of saved scenarios, so users can keep track of their runs.
This checks if scenarios is empty - and will only appear after the first scenario has been run.
We take the settings from each saved scenario and display them as a row in the table.
A caption reminds users that these scenarios are saved for the current session only.

if st.session_state.scenarios:

    st.header("Saved scenarios")

    st.dataframe(
        [scenario["settings"] for scenario in st.session_state.scenarios.values()],
        hide_index=True,
    )
    st.caption("Scenarios are saved for the current session only.")

Linking to results page
At the end of simulation.py, we’ll add a button linking to results.py, which we’ll create next.
Clicking the button calls st.switch_page to take the user to the results page.

st.subheader("Scenario summary")
st.write(f"""

Creating tabs



We have now finished the code for displaying results from one chosen scenario. Next, we’ll add a way to compare several scenarios.

We’ll use st.tabs to organise these two tasks within the results page:

View single scenario
Compare scenarios

Creating tabs


We pass st.tabs() a list with titles for each tab.

It returns a container for each tab, which we assign to variables (here, tab_single and tab_compare).

We then use a with block to add content to each tab.

st.title("View results")

if not st.session_state.scenarios:
    st.info("Run and save scenarios to view results here.", icon="ℹ️")

else:

        "You can either view results from a **single scenario**, or **compare across scenarios**."
    )

            st.info("Choose at least two scenario to compare", icon="ℹ️")

        else:
            # Results - will write next

Choosing scenarios to compare



2. Multiselect
Once there are at least two scenarios, we set up a container and create st.multiselect().
This is similar to selectbox, but allows users to choose multiple options at once.

with tab_compare:
    if len(st.session_state.scenarios) < 2:
        st.info("Run at least two scenarios to enable comparison", icon="ℹ️")

    else:
        st.space()
        with st.container(border=True):
            chosen_compare = st.multiselect(
                label="**Choose scenarios to compare**",
                options=list(st.session_state.scenarios),
            )

            st.caption("The selected scenarios are highlighted below.")

            st.dataframe(
                style_settings(settings=settings, chosen_scenarios=chosen_compare),
                hide_index=True,
            )

        if len(chosen_compare) < 2:
            st.info("Choose at least two scenario to compare", icon="ℹ️")

        else:
            # Results - will write next

Like before, we can show the saved scenarios and highlighted those selected using style_settings().

Show a message until at least two scenarios have been chosen. Then, results can be shown.

with tab_compare:
    if len(st.session_state.scenarios) < 2:

            # Results - will write next

Boxplot



Boxplots are a great option for comparing results across scenarios side by side.
They make it easy to see both the average results and the spread of results across replications.

Boxplot



1. Introduce figure
We’ll start by using st.subheader() and st.write() to introduce the figure and explain what it is showing.

st.subheader("Mean nurse queue time")
st.write(
    "Compare the mean nurse queue times across replications. "
    "Each point represents one replication."
)

# Combine replication results, adding a scenario label.
replications = pd.concat(
    [
        st.session_state.scenarios[name]["df"].assign(Scenario=name)
        for name in chosen_compare
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)

fig = px.box(
    replications,
    x="Scenario",
    y="mean_q_time_nurse",
    color="Scenario",
    points="all",
    category_orders={
        "Scenario": [
            name
            for name in st.session_state.scenarios
            if name in chosen_compare
        ]
    },
    hover_data=["replication_id"],
)
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis_title="Mean nurse queue time",
    showlegend=False,
)
st.plotly_chart(fig)

Boxplot



2. Create single results dataframe
Next, we use pd.concat() to stack the replication-level results from each scenario into a single dataframe called replications.
We also add a Scenario column to identify which scenario each row belongs to.

st.subheader("Mean nurse queue time")
st.write(
    "Compare the mean nurse queue times across replications. "
    "Each point represents one replication."
)

# Combine replication results, adding a scenario label.
replications = pd.concat(
    [
        st.session_state.scenarios[name]["df"].assign(Scenario=name)
        for name in chosen_compare
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)

fig = px.box(
    replications,
    x="Scenario",
    y="mean_q_time_nurse",
    color="Scenario",
    points="all",
    category_orders={
        "Scenario": [
            name
            for name in st.session_state.scenarios
            if name in chosen_compare
        ]
    },
    hover_data=["replication_id"],
)
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis_title="Mean nurse queue time",
    showlegend=False,
)
st.plotly_chart(fig)

Boxplot


3. Create boxplot
We create the figure using plotly.express.box():

color: group and color by scenario.
points: show each replication as a dot.
category_orders: keeps scenarios in the order they were saved.
hover_data: include replication IDs.

It’s displayed with st.plotly_chart().

st.subheader("Mean nurse queue time")
st.write(
    "Compare the mean nurse queue times across replications. "
    "Each point represents one replication."
)

# Combine replication results, adding a scenario label.
replications = pd.concat(
    [
        st.session_state.scenarios[name]["df"].assign(Scenario=name)
        for name in chosen_compare
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)

fig = px.box(
    replications,
    x="Scenario",
    y="mean_q_time_nurse",
    color="Scenario",
    points="all",
    category_orders={
        "Scenario": [
            name
            for name in st.session_state.scenarios
            if name in chosen_compare
        ]
    },
    hover_data=["replication_id"],
)
fig.update_layout(
    yaxis_title="Mean nurse queue time",
    showlegend=False,
)
st.plotly_chart(fig)

Comparison table
We could also use tables to compare results.

Comparison table



1. Construct summary table for nurse queue time
Here, we are creating a table with the descriptive statistics from each scenario.

st.space()
st.subheader("Summary statistics")

summary = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "Scenario": name,
            "Mean": st.session_state.scenarios[name]["mean"],
            "SD": st.session_state.scenarios[name]["sd"],
            "90th percentile": st.session_state.scenarios[name]["p90"],
            "Standard error": st.session_state.scenarios[name]["se"],
            "95% CI lower": st.session_state.scenarios[name][
                "ci_lower"
            ],
            "95% CI upper": st.session_state.scenarios[name][
                "ci_upper"
            ],
        }
        for name in chosen_compare
    ]
)

st.caption("Nurse queue time summary statistics, in minutes:")

st.dataframe(
    summary.style.format(precision=2),
    hide_index=True,
)

costs = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "Scenario": name,
            "Total cost (£)": st.session_state.scenarios[name]["cost"],
        }
        for name in chosen_compare
    ]
)

st.caption("Total nurse staffing costs:")

st.dataframe(costs, hide_index=True)

Comparison table

We then display it using st.dataframe(), with style.format() to round the numbers.
st.caption() provides some helpful context.

We can repeat this to show the nurse costs for each scenario. These are deterministic, just based on the number of resources in the simulation, so a single number is presented for each scenario.

Reminder: Streamlit Community Cloud
In the last session, we introduced Streamlit Community Cloud.
It was an easy way to deploy from GitHub, with automatic updates when you push changes.
However, apps share limited server resources and go to sleep after 12 hours without visitors.

stlite
An alternative is stlite, which runs Python directly in the user’s browser. Instead of sending requests to a server to run your code, the user’s own device does the work.

How does stlite work?


A browser can display your app, but can’t normally run its Python code. Browsers usually use JavaScript, a programming language designed for web pages.






In 2017, WebAssembly (Wasm) was released. It allows browsers to run compiled code alongside JavaScript, including software they wouldn’t normally support.







Pyodide uses WebAssembly to provide a Python environment. It includes an interpreter (which reads and runs Python code) and support for packages.







stlite uses this environment to run your Streamlit app on the user’s device.

stlite: pros and cons


Pros:

No server to wake up.
No external resource limits, can cope with concurrent users.
Data doesn’t leave the user’s browser.
Host for free with GitHub Pages.


Cons:

Initial loading can take longer while Python and packages download.
Slower to run (as depends on the user’s device).
Not all Python packages and Streamlit features are supported.
Set-up is not as easy as Streamlit Community Cloud.
Browser caching can leave users seeing an older version of the app.

Streamlit versions in stlite


stlite includes a modified version of Streamlit, adapted to run in the browser. This is why we do not add streamlit to <app-requirements>.

The stlite developers periodically update this version to the latest version of Streamlit, but may not always be up-to-date. New Streamlit features may therefore not be available immediately in stlite. Check the stlite release notes, and test your app before upgrading.


Each stlite release is pinned to a particular version of streamlit. For example, stlite 1.12.2 includes a build based on Streamlit 1.65.0.

section: Finding which streamlit version is in use
text:
Finding which streamlit version is in use


Via GitHub:

Open the stlite release you are using on GitHub.
Click the streamlit submodule link (e.g., streamlit @ 9c524f4). This opens the exact Streamlit source code included in that release.
Open lib/pyproject.toml and find version under [project].





Alternatively, run your app using your chosen stlite version and include this command to see which Streamlit build it uses:
st.write("Streamlit version:", st.__version__)

section: Try out the stlite app locally
text:
Try out the stlite app locally
index.html serves as the website’s starting page. To view the app locally, open a terminal in the folder containing index.html and run:
python -m http.server 8000
Then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser. This lets us test the app on our own computer.
To share it with others through a web address, we need to host its files online. GitHub Pages can host index.html and the other files our app needs. When someone visits the website, their browser downloads these files and runs the app using stlite.

GitHub Pages



GitHub Pages is a website hosting service. It takes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files from your GitHub repository and publishes them as a website.

It is free to use with public repositories.
It is easy to set up because it integrates directly with your GitHub repository.

Enabling GitHub Pages



The first step for setting up our stlite app website is to enable GitHub Pages.
From your GitHub repository, click on “Settings” and then in the sidebar click on “Pages”.

Enabling GitHub Pages
Under Source, select Deploy from a branch (if not already selected).
Then select main and / (root) and click Save.
It should now say your site is “currently being built from the main branch”.

Deployed site
Your app should now be live on GitHub Pages. Click the github-pages deployment in your repository’s right sidebar to view the deployment details and website link.

Add link to repository home
We’d recommend adding this link to your repository README.
You can also add it to the “About” panel by clicking the “⚙” symbol in the right sidebar, then clicking “Use your GitHub Pages website” and then “Save changes”.

File locations
These instructions assume your app files are in the repository root (the top-level folder).
This is why we selected / (root) when setting up GitHub Pages.
For example:
your-repository/
├── index.html
├── app.py
├── home.py
├── model.py
├── simulation.py
├── results.py
└── images/
    └── logo.png

File locations
You can also organise your app files into subfolders.
If index.html stays in the root, the GitHub Pages settings stay the same. Just update the paths in index.html to match your file locations.
For example:
your-repository/
├── index.html
└── app/
    ├── app.py
    ├── home.py
    ├── model.py
    ├── simulation.py
    ├── results.py
    └── images/
        └── logo.png

File locations
If you move index.html into a subfolder too, you have a few options:








Location
What to do




docs/index.html
Select main → /docs as the publishing source.


app/index.html
Publish the repository root and access the app at https://USERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY/app/.


app/index.html
Use a GitHub Actions workflow to publisht the contents of app/




For simplicity, we recommend keeping index.html in the repository root. The other files can be in subfolders - just make sure the paths in index.html match their locations.

All aboard the Enterprise



If you’re lucky enough to be working in a progressive organisation, you may have access to a service like Posit Connect, Plotly Dash Enterprise or Snowflake.



These services massively simplify the deployment and hosting of Streamlit apps, along with a series of bells and whistles like permission management/user authentication support.
It usually means someone else has already dealt with (most of) the messy stuff around secure sharing of data.

All aboard the Enterprise




For example, from Posit Connect, you can deploy Streamlit apps with just a few lines - as well as Shiny apps (in R or Python), Quarto documents (with scheduled refresh), Dash apps…

Name your price


Price - and/or the way pricing is calculated - can often be a barrier for organisations.

E.g., the “enhanced” tier of Posit Connect
However, the efficiency savings by working with a tool like this have the potential to be huge.
Posit in particular have some history of working with NHS organisations to make pricing available that will work.





Anyone using these? Shout out or pop it in the chat!

Customising app appearance
There’s lots of fun ways to change the appearance of your app!
We’re going to touch on a few of the options available…

st.set_page_config
This function configures the page’s appearance. Set defaults in app.py, then override them on individual pages if needed. Key parameters include…
page_title: The title shown in the browser tab.
page_icon: The favicon, which is a small icon beside the browser tab’s title. Use an image, emoji or Material Symbols icon.


import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(
    page_title="Nurse simulation",
    page_icon="🏥",
)

st.set_page_config
layout decides whether the app constrains content to a centered column (default) or if it uses the available page width.
This is what an app looks like with layout="centered".


import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(
    layout="centered"
)

with st.sidebar:
    st.title("Layout demo")

st.image("backtothefuture.png")

st.set_page_config
layout decides whether the app constrains content to a centered column (default) or if it uses the available page width.
This is what an app looks like with layout="wide".


import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(
    layout="wide"
)

with st.sidebar:
    st.title("Layout demo")

st.image("backtothefuture.png")

st.logo
This command creates a logo in the app. You can provide a path to an image, or an emoji or material symbols icon. For example:


import streamlit as st

st.logo("nihr_logo.png")

with st.sidebar:
    st.title("Logo demo")

st.write("This app has a logo in the sidebar")

st.navigation
When we set-up our multi-page app using st.navigation, it provided a navigation menu in a sidebar by default.
We can move the navigation menu to the top of the screen using position="top". For example:



import streamlit as st

pg = st.navigation(
    pages=[
        st.Page("page1.py"),
        st.Page("page2.py"),
    ],
    position="top",
)
pg.run()

config.toml
Create a .streamlit folder in your project folder, then add a config.toml file:
your-app/
├── app.py
└── .streamlit/
    └── config.toml
This is a configuration file. It can control things like logging, error messages, and caching.
We’ll focus now on using it to customise the app’s theme.

config.toml theme


[theme]

# Theme that your custom theme inherits from
# Can be Streamlit's default light or dark theme
# Or a local file path or URL to a custom theme.toml file
base = "light"

# Primary accent colour for interactive elements
primaryColor = "#2563EB"

#  Background colour for the main content area
backgroundColor = "#FFFCF5"

# Secondary background colour, used for widgets and the sidebar
secondaryBackgroundColor = "#DEEAF6"

# Default text colour
textColor = "#172B4D"

# Default font, excluding code
font = "sans-serif"

Define your theme settings under [theme]. There are lots of options - we have included a few of the main ones here.
Use [theme.sidebar] to override settings specifically for the sidebar.
You can also define separate light and dark themes using [theme.light] and [theme.dark].

config.toml theme: light
This is what the default light theme looks like.


[theme]

# Theme that your custom theme inherits from
# Can be Streamlit's default light or dark theme
# Or a local file path or URL to a custom theme.toml file
base = "light"

config.toml theme: dark
This is what the default dark theme looks like.


[theme]

# Theme that your custom theme inherits from
# Can be Streamlit's default light or dark theme
# Or a local file path or URL to a custom theme.toml file
base = "dark"

config.toml theme: custom
This is an example of a custom theme.


[theme]

# Theme that your custom theme inherits from
# Can be Streamlit's default light or dark theme
# Or a local file path or URL to a custom theme.toml file
base = "light"

# Primary accent colour for interactive elements
primaryColor = "#2563EB"

#  Background colour for the main content area
backgroundColor = "#FFFCF5"

# Secondary background colour, used for widgets and the sidebar
secondaryBackgroundColor = "#DEEAF6"

# Default text colour
textColor = "#172B4D"

# Default font, excluding code
font = "sans-serif"

CSS
For additional customisation, we can use CSS (Cascading Style Sheets). CSS is a language that controls how web content look.
Use config.toml for the overall theme, and Streamlit’s built-in options wherever possible. CSS is useful for more specific styling that these options don’t support.
We can write these styles in a .css file and load them into our app using st.html().
import streamlit as st

with open("style.css") as css:
    st.html(f"<style>{css.read()}</style>")
Streamlit has introduced lots of new features over the last few years. You may find older tutorial using CSS, but those features are now supported directly by Streamlit, so it’s always worth checking the current documentaiton.
